rationale: Plain range cannot tell a stock that is always volatile from one whose range has just jumped against its own last quarter; the jump marks new uncertainty that the level has not yet fully reflected. Range stays the core, the own-history z-score is a small tilt.

The lowest range a stock reached in a quarter shows whether its volatility is structural or a passing episode; a high floor means the risk never went away, which should matter more over a one-year horizon than today's reading.

Two stocks with the same range differ if one is already far below its year high: the fall has raised its leverage and shaken its holders, information about state that range does not contain. Small weight so it does not drown the core as the equal-weight trend blend did.

The 50/200-day spread is the slowest trend measure available and turns negative only after a sustained deterioration; at equal weight trend diluted range, so this tests whether a light tilt toward broken long trends adds anything at all.
Range is direction-free; a quarter in which volume concentrated on down days says the turbulence is being produced by sellers, which is the kind that precedes large falls rather than large rallies.

Where the close sits inside the daily range is exactly the information the range throws away; a quarter of closes near the lows means each day's range was resolved downward, i.e. persistent selling into the close.

The worst opening gap of the quarter records a discrete bad-news event (earnings miss, guidance cut, legal shock); a 14-day average range forgets it within weeks, while such events tend to come in series.

The least traded index members are the smallest and closest to deletion, with fewer buyers when holders want out; for the same range their falls go further, and dollar volume is not a volatility measure so it should not simply duplicate the core.
A last quarter that was much worse than the one before means the stock's situation is deteriorating at an increasing rate; range reports the turbulence but not whether the path is bending downward.

The share of a quarter's variance that came from down days separates volatility made of bad news from volatility made of good news; the same range is more dangerous when most of it was earned on the way down.

A stock within 5% of its 52-week low has no recent buyers in profit and is where stop-losses and mandate-driven selling sit; the same range is scaled up by half there, leaving the ranking by range intact everywhere else.
Volume rising above its half-year average means ownership is turning over; a wide range together with a change of hands signals that long-term holders are leaving, which range alone cannot show.

A large one-year loss is the market's own verdict on the business and raises financial leverage mechanically; it is the return leg of a distance-to-default measure, added here lightly instead of at the full weight that failed before.

When a large part of a stock's movement happens between close and open it is driven by discrete news rather than trading noise; news-driven risk produces the jumps that make up most 25% falls, and the gap share is independent of the range level.

The largest volume spike of the quarter marks a company that has had a major event; event-prone companies keep having events, and a single day of five times normal volume barely moves a 14-day average range.
The worst 20-day return inside the last quarter shows whether the stock has already had one crash; crashes cluster, and after the range has calmed the memory of that month is the only trace left.

The share of the last quarter spent below the 50-day average measures how persistent the weakness is, not how deep; a volatile stock that cannot get back above its average for months is being sold steadily.

A very large one-year move in either direction means the valuation has been repriced hard and is unsettled: big losers can go to zero and big winners have furthest to fall. This adds a yearly-scale instability measure that a 14-day range cannot see.

Trend strength signed by direction separates a volatile stock in an orderly, strong decline from one that is merely noisy; a strong directional decline is price discovery of bad news rather than turbulence.

Range beat close-to-close volatility by 0.037, so the part of range that closes do not show may be where the information is: large intraday swings that reverse by the close indicate thin order books and disagreement, typical of stressed names.

A one-year outcome depends on the stock's lasting volatility level, and a 14-day average still carries the noise of the last few weeks; averaging it over a quarter should be a cleaner estimate of the same quantity.

The highest range reached in the quarter shows how turbulent the stock can become under stress; a stock that has calmed down since an episode is ranked low by current range although it has just shown what it is capable of.

Taking the larger of the current and the quarterly range reacts at once when risk rises but does not forget when it falls, matching the asymmetry of risk: volatility spikes fast and decays slowly in its consequences.

Two consecutive quarterly averages give roughly a half-year range, the longest direct average the language allows; if longer smoothing is better because the target is a full year ahead, this should improve again on the quarterly mean.

Overnight gaps cannot be traded out of and are where most single-day collapses occur; adding the average gap size to the range gives overnight movement extra weight relative to intraday movement in the same units.

A downside-only volatility over a quarter measures exactly the kind of movement the target is about and ignores turbulence from rallies; if the direction of volatility matters this should beat a direction-free range.

Close-to-close volatility lost to range when both were short-window estimates, but averaged over a quarter it is a far less noisy and partly independent reading of the same risk; at a third of the weight it can only refine the core.

The geometric mean of current and quarterly range requires both to be high for a top score, damping one-off spikes and stale averages alike; it is the balanced alternative to taking the worse of the two.

Scaling the quarterly range by the 5-to-60-day range ratio approximates a 5-day range, the fastest estimate available; it tests the opposite direction to the longer averages, in case the freshest information is what carries the signal.

The calmest reading of the quarter is a robust estimate of permanent volatility, untouched by any episode; if falls come from structurally volatile businesses rather than from recent turbulence, the floor alone should rank better than the current value.

Dividing by the ratio of current band width to its own 250-day mean removes the part of range that is unusual for this stock and leaves its year-typical level, the only way in this language to reach a one-year volatility estimate that matches the horizon of the target.

The mean absolute daily return over a quarter is a close-to-close estimate that is robust to single outliers and three times longer than vol20; it shows whether vol20 lost to range because closes carry less information or only because its window was short and squared.

An average describes ordinary days, while a 25% fall is a tail outcome; adding the largest single-day move of the quarter to the quarterly range brings in the fatness of the tail, which two stocks with the same average can differ on.

Only downward opening gaps are added to the range, at double weight: they are the footprints of bad news released outside trading hours, and a stock that keeps opening lower is being repriced on fundamentals rather than traded noisily.

Volatility measured on weekly returns keeps moves that persist across days and cancels daily back-and-forth; a year-long fall is made of persistent moves, so the lower-frequency estimate may be closer to the risk that matters than any daily range.

As a product, trend cannot lift a calm stock to the top the way the equal-weight sum did: the score is high only when range is high and the stock is below its 200-day, so it tests whether range is more dangerous in a downtrend without diluting it.

Illiquidity scales the range between half and one and a half times instead of adding to it: in a thinly traded member the same turbulence meets fewer buyers, so the conversion of volatility into a large fall should be higher.

If the stock lost more than 20% in some month of the last quarter, the score uses the quarter's peak range instead of the current one; after a crash the calm that follows is unreliable and should not be allowed to lower the estimate.

A wide range on rising volume is repricing with real participation, while a wide range on falling volume is a thin market moving on little trade; scaling by the volume trend separates the two for the same range.

The product is high only when the stock is volatile and its variance sits on down days; it removes from the top of the ranking the volatile stocks whose turbulence came from rallies, which a sum would only partly do.

Below the 200-day a fresh jump in range is likely the start of something and is taken at once (the worse of current and quarterly); above it a jump is more often an earnings-day blip and only the quarterly average is used.

Dividing by the price as a fraction of its year high scales the range up in proportion to the drawdown: a company whose equity has shrunk carries more debt per unit of equity, so the same range means more distress the further it has fallen.

The range is multiplied by a factor that runs from near zero when closes sit at the daily highs to near two when they sit at the lows, turning a direction-free range into the part of the range that sellers won over the quarter.

The current range is discounted by how much the stock's range varied over the quarter: a reading that is high and has been steadily high counts in full, one that is a spike inside a wide band of readings counts less.

A stock is ranked by whichever is worse, its range or its average overnight gap: some companies trade quietly during the day but reprice in jumps at the open, and an either-or rule catches them without lowering anyone flagged by range.

The range is scaled by whether it is currently expanding or contracting against its 60-day level, clipped so the adjustment stays modest; expanding risk is under-stated by a trailing average and contracting risk is over-stated.
When down-day volume has clearly dominated for two months the range is scaled up by 30%; the switch only acts on stocks under sustained selling and leaves the range ordering untouched for all others.

Volatile and sitting on its 52-week low is a different state from volatile and well above it: the first has no cushion and no holders in profit, the second is often a recovery. The product keeps only the first at the top.

Range is scaled up at both ends of the trend ranking, for stocks collapsing below their 200-day and for stocks stretched far above it; a wide range in an over-extended stock is a blow-off, which a one-directional trend term would wrongly mark as safe.

The ratio of the quarter's largest daily move to its average daily move measures how jump-like the stock's risk is; for the same average range, a stock that moves in jumps is the one that can lose a quarter of its value on one announcement.

The ratio of the 52-week low to the 52-week high is a realised one-year range, the only volatility estimate here measured over the same horizon as the target; if a year-long measure is what matters it could beat a 14-day one without using it.

Built from pieces range does not use directly: a quarter of close-to-close volatility, average overnight gap size and the drawdown from the year high. If these three together match range14, range is one view of volatility; if not, the intraday range itself is special.

Close-to-close volatility with the band-width ratio divided out approximates the stock's year-typical volatility; it tests whether vol20 lost to range14 because of its short window rather than because closes are less informative.

The largest weekly move of the quarter is a tail measure at a frequency where moves are no longer noise; companies that have produced a 15% week are the ones able to produce a 25% year, whatever their average day looks like.

Both parts look only at the downside: how far the stock already is below its year high and how violent its down days have been. It asks whether a purely downside description of risk does better than a direction-free range.

The average size of opening gaps over a quarter measures risk that arrives as news outside trading hours and nothing else; if large falls are mostly news events, this single component could rank companies as well as the full range.

Quarterly close-to-close volatility plus a half-weight tilt to the least traded members: size and trading depth are the non-volatility facts most related to who gets hurt, and this checks whether they can make up for not having the intraday range.

A distance-to-default style measure without range: high sustained volatility and a price below its long average, as a product so both are required. Earlier this kind of measure did not beat volatility as a sum; the product form is the remaining untested version.

The realised one-year high-low range with a light tilt toward stocks sitting near the bottom of it: a wide year that is being resolved downward. Uses only yearly components, so it is the slowest-moving risk measure in the set.

A deliberate control with no volatility term at all: trend, trading depth, down-day volume and weak closes. It measures how far everything that is not volatility can go, which shows whether the additions in group A have anything to contribute.
